annotation_description: Playing Bloodstained Mire instead of Swamp wastes 1 life when cracking the fetch, and the player wants to cast Thoughtseize (costs B) or Faithless Looting (costs R) this turn. If they play Swamp, they can cast Thoughtseize immediately for free (no life from fetch). If they play Bloodstained Mire, they need to crack it (paying 1 life) to get a Swamp to cast Thoughtseize, losing 1 unnecessary life point. The fetch land should be saved for later when color flexibility is actually needed or when revolt for Fatal Push matters. Playing Swamp directly and saving the fetchland preserves life and keeps open the option to trigger revolt with Bloodstained Mire on a future turn when Fatal Push needs to hit a 3-4 mana value creature.

Playing Swamp instead of using Bloodstained Mire is slightly suboptimal. The player has Faithless Looting in hand which they likely want to cast soon to fill the graveyard for Abhorrent Oculus. By cracking Bloodstained Mire for a Swamp (or Mountain), they would get a permanent leaving the battlefield, enabling Revolt for Fatal Push to hit creatures with mana value 4 or less - relevant against the opponent's potential threats like Atraxa. Additionally, thinning the deck and having the fetch available to crack at instant speed on the opponent's turn provides more flexibility. Playing the Swamp from hand preserves the fetch but wastes the opportunity to keep options open - they should save the Swamp for a turn when they have no fetch to play.

With two Fatal Pushes in hand, Bloodstained Mire should be preserved on the battlefield to enable Revolt on a future turn (allowing Fatal Push to kill creatures with mana value 4 or less, critical against threats like Atraxa). Playing the Swamp from hand achieves the same goal of casting Thoughtseize this turn while preserving the fetch land's Revolt utility.

Llama4 Johnny has Bloodstained Mire on the battlefield and a Swamp in hand, with Thoughtseize in hand (which costs {B}). They need to play the Swamp (or crack the Bloodstained Mire to fetch a Swamp) to cast Thoughtseize this turn. Instead, they passed without playing a land, missing their turn 2 land drop entirely. This means they can't cast Thoughtseize on turn 2, losing a critical tempo window to strip an important card from the opponent's hand (like Atraxa or other threats). The reasoning that 'Thoughtseize is not available to cast right now' is wrong — they simply needed to play the Swamp from hand to have access to {B} mana. Additionally, by not playing the Swamp, they'll be forced to discard to hand size (going from 8 to 7), losing a card for free.

message: Select a Swamp or Mountain card
annotation_description: Fetching Undercity Sewers off Bloodstained Mire means the land enters tapped, costing a mana this turn cycle. The player has Faithless Looting (R), Thoughtseize (B), and Fatal Push (B) they might want to cast. Blood Crypt or Steam Vents could enter untapped (paying 2 life) and provide immediate mana access. Blood Crypt would give both B and R, enabling Thoughtseize or Faithless Looting immediately. The surveil 1 from Undercity Sewers has marginal value compared to having an untapped land. Additionally, the player already has a Swamp in hand they could play next turn for black mana, so getting an untapped dual now would be more valuable for tempo.

Discarding Polluted Delta instead of a less useful card wastes a land that could enable Revolt for Fatal Push (by sacrificing it) and help fix mana. With only one land on the battlefield (Undercity Sewers) and needing to develop mana, a fetchland is quite valuable. Meanwhile, the player has two copies of Thoughtseize which are less critical at this stage, and discarding a duplicate Thoughtseize would preserve mana development options.

With 4 lands about to be available (3 on board + Island being played), the player could have cast Faithful Mending (WU) to draw 2, discard 2, and gain 2 life. This would help fill the graveyard and dig toward lands/answers, potentially setting up an earlier Atraxa or finding more action. Faithful Mending at end of opponent's turn would be better, but since it's postcombat main and they chose to just play a land, they're passing up the option to cast Faithful Mending this turn (they could cast it on opponent's end step next turn instead with 4 mana). However, casting Faithful Mending on the opponent's end step next turn is arguably better since it keeps mana open and the Island play is fine. The real question is whether Quantum Riddler via Warp {1}{U} could have been cast - but they only have 4 mana total after playing Island, and Warp costs {1}{U} = 2 mana, which means it enters as a 2/2 face-down creature. Actually, playing Island and passing to use Faithful Mending on opponent's end step is quite reasonable. This is a close call but likely fine play.

Casting Quantum Riddler (via Warp for 1U) instead of Faithful Mending (WU) on turn 4 with 4 mana available. Faithful Mending would draw 2 cards, discard 2, gain 2 life, and help fill the graveyard to set up future plays like Abhorrent Oculus or fuel graveyard synergies. It also leaves mana open for potential interaction. The Quantum Riddler as a 2/2 face-down creature (Warp puts it face-down as a 2/2 manifest) only draws a card when it enters face-up. Actually, looking more carefully at Warp - Warp {1}{U} manifests the creature, putting it face down as a 2/2. It doesn't trigger the ETB draw. However, you can later pay its full mana cost to flip it face up and get the ETB trigger. The question is whether a 2/2 body now is better than Faithful Mending's card filtering and life gain. With the opponent at low pressure (only an Undercity Sewers tapped, no creatures), Faithful Mending to dig toward answers and set up the graveyard for later flashback seems reasonable. But a 2/2 body that can later flip into a 4/6 flyer with card draw is also fine. This is debatable but Faithful Mending at end of opponent's turn would have been more flexible, preserving the option to cast Riddler later while getting card selection now.

After playing Swamp, the player had 2 black mana available (Undercity Sewers + Swamp) but cast nothing and skipped to attacks. They could have cast Unearth targeting Psychic Frog (mana value 2, eligible) for {B} to recover their key win condition, and still had {B} remaining for Thoughtseize to strip the opponent's hand. The opponent had multiple tapped lands, making this an ideal window to deploy threats and disrupt.

message: Select card to discard (selected 0 of 2, min 2)
annotation_description: Grok4F ESPN is discarding Psychic Frog to Faithful Mending when they should be discarding Atraxa, Grand Unifier. The entire game plan revolves around using Goryo's Vengeance to reanimate Atraxa from the graveyard. They already have two copies of Atraxa in hand and Goryo's Vengeance ready to go. Discarding Atraxa would set up a turn 5 or soon thereafter Goryo's Vengeance → Atraxa line, which is one of the most powerful things this deck can do. Psychic Frog is a fine card but much less impactful than the Goryo's + Atraxa combo. They already discarded one card (likely the first discard was fine), but discarding Psychic Frog over Atraxa for the second discard misses the primary reanimation plan.

Llama4 Johnny used Thoughtseize to take Ephemerate from Grok4F ESPN's hand, but the opponent's hand contains Goryo's Vengeance and TWO copies of Atraxa, Grand Unifier. Goryo's Vengeance is the most dangerous card here — it can instantly reanimate Atraxa (which is legendary) at instant speed, creating a 7/7 with flying, vigilance, deathtouch, lifelink that draws ~4-5 cards on ETB. The opponent already has a Psychic Frog in graveyard and could discard an Atraxa to set up Goryo's Vengeance. Ephemerate is relatively low-impact when the opponent has no creatures on board. Taking Goryo's Vengeance removes the explosive reanimation threat, while taking Ephemerate does almost nothing meaningful.

Took one of two Ataxas instead of the single Goryo's Vengeance, leaving the opponent's reanimation combo fully intact. Opponent still has Atraxa + Goryo's Vengeance + Ephemerate, meaning they can discard Atraxa via Faithful Mending and immediately Goryo's Vengeance it into play, then Ephemerate to keep it permanently.

Grok4F ESPN passed on casting Goryo's Vengeance to reanimate Atraxa, Grand Unifier from the graveyard during combat. With the opponent at 15 life, no blockers, and all lands tapped, Atraxa would attack as a 7/7 flying haste lifelinker for 7 damage (opponent to 8), gain 7 life, and trigger ETB to draw up to 8 cards across card types. Additionally, Ephemerate in hand could blink Atraxa to remove the 'exile at end step' clause, keeping Atraxa permanently and triggering another ETB. This is the deck's signature combo line.

Grok4F ESPN has the Goryo's Vengeance + Ephemerate combo available with Atraxa in the graveyard and opponent completely tapped out. Goryo's Vengeance ({1}{B}) reanimates Atraxa for a massive ETB, then Ephemerate ({W}) blinks her to dodge the exile clause and trigger ETB again, with rebound providing a third trigger next upkeep. This is a game-winning line against a tapped-out opponent with no board.

message: Select a card of each card type (selected 0)
annotation_description: From Atraxa's ETB reveal, chose a second Atraxa, Grand Unifier as the creature pick when Solitude was available. They already have Atraxa on the battlefield and another in hand (legendary, so redundant). Solitude can be evoked for free by exiling a white card (they have Ephemerate and March of Otherworldly Light in hand) and provides crucial removal/interaction.

message: Select card to discard (selected 0 of 2, min 2)
annotation_description: Discarding Goryo's Vengeance instead of a second Atraxa wastes the reanimation synergy. If the on-board Atraxa is removed, they now need to hardcast a 7-mana creature with only 4-5 lands instead of having a 2-mana instant-speed reanimation spell. Discarding Atraxa to the graveyard would have made it a perfect Goryo's Vengeance target.

Cast Thoughtseize before playing Polluted Delta. Should play the land first to have more mana available and maintain better sequencing. With only 4 lands and needing to reach 7 for Atraxa, every land drop matters. Playing the land first also enables cracking it for revolt if needed and provides an additional mana source for potential responses.

Cast Faithful Mending before playing Polluted Delta. Playing the land first preserves flexibility: if Faithful Mending draws a land they'd prefer to play this turn, that option is lost. Additionally, having Polluted Delta on the battlefield gives the option to crack it for revolt or additional mana (potentially enabling 3 mana for more plays).

Fetched Watery Grave (U/B) when they already have access to U and B mana. They have two Atraxa, Grand Unifier in hand which requires green mana (3GWUB), and Hedge Maze was available as their only green source. All lands were tapped anyway, so the 2 life paid to get Watery Grave untapped was wasted value. Without green mana, casting Atraxa becomes much harder.

message: Select card to discard (selected 0 of 2, min 2)
annotation_description: Discarded the last copy of Goryo's Vengeance from hand, putting all 3 copies in the graveyard where they can't be cast. This eliminates the Goryo's Vengeance + Ephemerate combo on Atraxa, which is the deck's primary game plan. Without Goryo's in hand, they have no way to cheat Atraxa into play.

Fatal Push cannot destroy Quantum Riddler because it has mana value 5, which exceeds both the base threshold (2 or less) and the revolt threshold (4 or less). Even if revolt were active (no permanent left the battlefield this turn), 5 > 4. This wastes a removal spell on an illegal/ineffective target. The card should have been saved or Bitter Triumph should have been used instead if removing Quantum Riddler was important.

Fatal Push cannot destroy Quantum Riddler (mana value 5) even with Revolt (which only raises the threshold to 4). The Fatal Push on the stack will resolve and do nothing. Meanwhile, Bitter Triumph could actually destroy Quantum Riddler by discarding a card.

Unearth on Psychic Frog is a weak play here. The opponent has a 4/6 Quantum Riddler on board and all their lands are tapped. Bitter Triumph can destroy the Quantum Riddler right now while the opponent is tapped out and unable to respond with countermagic. Psychic Frog as a 1/2 doesn't meaningfully pressure through a 4/6 flyer, and Llama4 Johnny would need to discard cards to pump it or give it flying. Meanwhile, the Quantum Riddler is a significant threat that draws extra cards when the opponent is low on hand size. Using Bitter Triumph now (discarding Archon of Cruelty, which can later be reanimated or is otherwise hard to cast) to kill the Riddler while the opponent is tapped out is a much stronger line.

message: Select a creature card with mana value 3 or less from your graveyard
annotation_description: Abhorrent Oculus has mana value 3 and is a legal Unearth target. It would provide a 5/5 flyer plus manifest dread triggers on opponent's upkeep, which is dramatically more impactful than a 1/2 Psychic Frog that requires additional discard investment to grow. The opponent's lands are all tapped so there's no risk difference.

Discarding Bitter Triumph removes the only removal spell in hand, while Archon of Cruelty is an 8-mana creature that is extremely unlikely to be hardcast with only 4 lands in play and no reanimation targets set up (no way to get it into the graveyard and reanimate it since Unearth can only target MV 3 or less, and there are no Goryo's Vengeance in hand). Bitter Triumph is a flexible instant-speed removal spell that could answer the opponent's Quantum Riddler or future threats. Discarding Archon of Cruelty instead would pump the Frog equally while keeping the removal spell, and the Archon in the graveyard could potentially be reanimated later if a Goryo's Vengeance is drawn (it's legendary, making it a valid target).

Grok4F ESPN responded to their own Thoughtseize (on the stack, targeting Llama4 Johnny) by casting March of Otherworldly Light to exile Psychic Frog. This is poor sequencing - Thoughtseize would resolve first, letting ESPN see Llama4 Johnny's hand and potentially take a key card (like a counterspell or threat). By casting March now in response to their own spell, they spend mana and a card before getting the information from Thoughtseize. Additionally, March of Otherworldly Light for X=1 costs {1}{W}, but they could have cast it after Thoughtseize resolved, using the hand information to decide whether the Frog was even the right target or if there was a bigger threat to worry about. Furthermore, by using March here they're spending mana that could be relevant for Force of Negation backup or other plays. The Psychic Frog is a real threat worth removing, but the sequencing wastes the information advantage from Thoughtseize.

Opponent cast Thoughtseize targeting Grok4F ESPN. Grok4F ESPN has Force of Negation in hand and it's not their turn (wait - actually it IS their turn, turn 9 belongs to Grok4F ESPN). But looking more carefully: the Thoughtseize is on the stack, and Grok4F ESPN is responding. Since it's Grok4F ESPN's own turn, Force of Negation cannot be cast for its alternate cost (exile a blue card). Force of Negation costs 1UU to hardcast, and ESPN has 4 lands tapped out of 6 (Shadowy Backstreet, Island, Watery Grave, Plains are tapped; Hallowed Fountain and Godless Shrine are untapped). Hallowed Fountain produces W or U, Godless Shrine produces W or B - that's only 2 mana available, not enough for 1UU. So Force of Negation can't be cast here. The choices given are Force of Negation and three Faithful Mendings (flashback from graveyard). Wait - but actually Thoughtseize is a sorcery, so if it's being cast on ESPN's turn... Actually, looking at the board state, Llama4 Johnny has tapped lands too. Let me reconsider - the Thoughtseize on the stack was likely cast by Llama4 Johnny on a previous turn's resolution, or ESPN cast it targeting themselves? No - ESPN is the active player and the message says 'Play instants and activated abilities' in response to Thoughtseize on the stack. ESPN chose Faithful Mending (flashback) instead of letting Thoughtseize resolve. Faithful Mending costs 1WU to flashback. With Hallowed Fountain (W/U) and Godless Shrine (W/B) untapped, ESPN can produce WU or WW or WB - not enough for 1WU (needs 3 mana, only 2 lands untapped). Actually wait, the choice was offered so presumably it's legal. The real question is whether responding with Faithful Mending to Thoughtseize is correct. By casting Faithful Mending, ESPN draws 2 cards and discards 2, gaining 2 life, BEFORE Thoughtseize resolves. This gives the opponent more information and more cards to choose from when Thoughtseize resolves. It would have been better to let Thoughtseize resolve first (opponent sees current hand and takes a card), then flashback Faithful Mending afterward to potentially draw replacements. By casting Mending first, opponent gets to see the refreshed hand including new draws.

message: Select card to discard (selected 0 of 2, min 2)
annotation_description: Discarded Thoughtseize instead of the second Force of Negation. Thoughtseize is efficient 1-mana proactive disruption that's easy to cast. The second Force of Negation would be difficult to cast for its alternate cost since the only blue card remaining in hand would be Atraxa (their win condition they don't want to exile). Hard-casting Force at 1UU is also demanding. Thoughtseize provides more practical utility in the current game state.

message: You may choose an alternative cost
chosen_display: Cast with Evoke alternative cost: Exile a white card from your hand (source: <font color='#F0E68C' object_id='3d519e53-fa91-4da3-bd9f-c573dadf5459'>Solitude</font> [3d5])
annotation_description: Evoked Solitude by exiling Atraxa, Grand Unifier from hand with no enemy creatures on the battlefield to exile. This wastes both Solitude and Atraxa (two cards) to accomplish nothing. The opponent has Thoughtseize on the stack which would only take one card. By evoking Solitude, they lose two cards instead of one.

Grok4F ESPN chose to discard Archon of Cruelty with Thoughtseize, but Llama4 Johnny's graveyard is already stocked with reanimation-friendly cards and Johnny has no way to cheat Archon into play from hand with only 3 lands (2 untapped). The two Faithless Lootings are far more dangerous - they let Johnny dig for threats, fill the graveyard further, and find answers. With Faithless Looting, Johnny can draw into reanimation spells, more threats, or disruption while also fueling graveyard synergies. Archon of Cruelty costs 8 mana and Johnny is on 3 lands with no ramp visible - it's extremely unlikely to be hardcast anytime soon. Meanwhile, Faithless Looting (especially with flashback) provides consistent card selection and graveyard filling that enables Johnny's entire game plan. Taking a Faithless Looting would have been more impactful at slowing Johnny's development.

message: Select up to one card from a graveyard
annotation_description: Emperor of Bones exiles a card from a graveyard at the beginning of combat, and when it gets +1/+1 counters (via Adapt 2 for {1}{B}), it puts an exiled creature card onto the battlefield with haste. The player exiled Thoughtseize, a sorcery, which cannot be put onto the battlefield as a creature. The opponent's graveyard contains Atraxa, Grand Unifier and Solitude - extremely powerful creatures that could be reanimated with Emperor of Bones' adapt ability. Even from the player's own graveyard, Archon of Cruelty or Abhorrent Oculus would be high-impact targets. Exiling a sorcery wastes the Emperor's key ability entirely.

Casting Faithful Mending flashback during own combat step rather than waiting until end of opponent's turn. While it could draw cards for main phase 2, holding it preserves more information and flexibility. With two Force of Negations already providing protection, the reactive gameplan favors waiting to see what the opponent does before spending mana and making discard decisions.

message: Select card to discard (selected 0 of 2, min 2)
annotation_description: Discarding Force of Negation and Psychic Frog while keeping Ephemerate and Atraxa. The opponent (Llama4 Johnny) has Emperor of Bones on the battlefield and multiple high-value reanimation targets in their graveyard including Archon of Cruelty and Abhorrent Oculus. Force of Negation is one of the few ways to interact with the opponent's spells on their turn for free, and all of Grok4F ESPN's lands are tapped. While keeping Atraxa as a potential Goryo's Vengeance target or hard cast makes sense, discarding both copies of Force of Negation (one here, potentially drawing into needing them later) leaves Grok4F ESPN vulnerable. However, since all lands are tapped and this is during combat on Grok4F ESPN's own turn, the defensive value of Force of Negation is somewhat diminished in the immediate term. Keeping Ephemerate to rebuy ETB triggers is reasonable. This is debatable but losing both free counterspells when the opponent has threatening lines is concerning.

message: Select up to one card from a graveyard
annotation_description: Emperor of Bones triggers at the beginning of combat, exiling a card from a graveyard, and when it gets +1/+1 counters (via Adapt 2 for 1B), it puts a creature exiled with it onto the battlefield with haste and a finality counter. Exiling Gran-Gran (a 1/2) is far weaker than exiling Archon of Cruelty (a 6/6 with a devastating ETB trigger that makes the opponent sacrifice a creature/planeswalker, discard a card, lose 3 life, and draws you a card and gains 3 life) or Atraxa, Grand Unifier (a 7/7 with flying, vigilance, deathtouch, lifelink and a powerful ETB). When Emperor of Bones adapts, bringing back Archon of Cruelty or Atraxa even for one turn would be game-changing, while Gran-Gran provides minimal value as a 1/2 that draws/discards when tapped.

Copied Solitude with Superior Spider-Man instead of Archon of Cruelty from opponent's graveyard. Solitude's exile trigger gives the opponent life equal to Emperor of Bones' power, while Archon's ETB forces opponent to sacrifice a creature (removing Emperor anyway), discard a card, lose 3 life, AND draws you a card and gains you 3 life. With Ephemerate in hand for a second ETB trigger, Archon is dramatically better.

message: Select card to discard (selected 0 of 2, min 2)
annotation_description: At 2 life facing an opponent at 29 life with a developed board, the player discarded Abhorrent Oculus (a 5/5 flyer for 3 mana that generates tokens each turn) and kept Ragavan (a 2/1 that's poor when behind and can't profitably attack into Superior Spider-Man with reach). Abhorrent Oculus was castable next turn with 14 cards in graveyard and was by far the most impactful card to stabilize from a losing position.

At 2 life facing a 4/4 Superior Spider-Man, casting Ragavan (a 2/1 that can't attack profitably into the 4/4) is suboptimal when Emperor of Bones offers better defensive and offensive utility. Emperor of Bones can exile powerful creatures from the opponent's graveyard (like Atraxa or Solitude) and potentially reanimate them. Additionally, both creatures could have been cast in the same turn using all 4 available mana, or Faithless Looting flashback could have been used to dig for critical answers at 2 life.

message: You may choose an alternative cost
chosen_display: Cast with Dash alternative cost: {1}{R} (source: <font color='#FF6347' object_id='583c1fa6-53a3-441c-ab26-e44d5dbfb8c2'>Ragavan, Nimble Pilferer</font> [583])
annotation_description: At 2 life with only Emperor of Bones in hand, Llama4 Johnny chose to Dash Ragavan for {1}{R} instead of casting it normally for {R}. Dashing costs an extra mana (using Blood Crypt + Island instead of just Blood Crypt) and returns Ragavan to hand at end of turn, meaning it won't stick as a blocker. At 2 life against an opponent with Superior Spider-Man (a 4/4) and potential attacks, having a permanent blocker could be critical for survival. The 'dash benefit' of haste is irrelevant since Ragavan has no summoning sickness issues for attacking this turn anyway — wait, Ragavan doesn't have haste naturally, so Dash does grant haste. However, spending 2 mana instead of 1 leaves less mana open, and more importantly, Ragavan bounces back to hand at end of turn, so it can't block next turn. At 2 life, a permanent 2/1 body that can block is far more valuable than the tempo of dashing, especially when you also want to cast Emperor of Bones ({1}{B}) and may not have mana for both. By dashing for {1}{R}, you use Blood Crypt + Island, leaving Swamp + Undercity Sewers, which is enough for Emperor of Bones. But next turn you'd need to recast Ragavan again. Casting normally for {R} saves mana and keeps the body on board as a potential blocker.
